title: The Problems With Pace
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins confesses to having given lazy "improve your pace" feedback after lesson observations for years, and uses this post to dismantle pace as a meaningful piece of classroom feedback. His central argument is that pace is both poorly defined and impossible to judge fairly from a snapshot observation, since an observer walking into the middle of a lesson has no way to know whether a teacher labouring a point is responding to a genuine gap in understanding or just dragging. He proposes replacing "pace" with more granular, falsifiable diagnoses - is this a checking-for-understanding problem, or an explanation-clarity problem - so that feedback conversations can actually lead somewhere. Robbins also tackles the curriculum-pace conflation, arguing that rushing through content to "cover the course" often just defers the problem, since insecure early learning forces repeated re-teaching later; he suggests, via the Matthew effect, that a slower, more secure start can be faster in aggregate. He doesn't pretend the tension disappears entirely - departments still face real time constraints and sometimes have to "cut their losses" pragmatically with some students - but insists that professional judgement should replace the reflexive appeal to an undefined word like pace.
points: Robbins' core complaint about "pace" as classroom-observation feedback is that it's simultaneously vague and unfalsifiable - an observer can't judge whether a lesson is too slow or too fast without knowing what happened before they walked in.

He reframes "slow pace" complaints as two distinct, actionable problems in disguise: a ratio issue (not enough students thinking hard) or a time-management issue (students could finish faster) - and argues good feedback should name which one it actually is.

Robbins invokes the Matthew effect to argue that teaching more slowly early on, so concepts become secure, saves time later by reducing the need for re-teaching - meaning slow pace can be the faster long-term strategy.

He acknowledges a tension: departments still have to cover a curriculum in fixed time, so pace decisions ultimately require professional judgement about which students to prioritise when trade-offs are unavoidable.
quotes: When people say the pace of a lesson is two slow they often mean that there is too much dead time whereby students are not being asked to think hard enough (A ratio issue) or the students could have finished the same work in a shorter time
So instead of using the word ‘pace’ we need to think carefully about what is actually the problem and be more granular. Is it actually that the students got it earlier

As observers we owe it to the teachers we see to help them develop. If we can avoid using these poorly defined words like pace (and engagement) then we are one step closer to fulfilling out obligation.
What if we taught a bit slower but provided more opportunities for students to think hard about ideas, so they became more permanent and therefore needed less re-teaching?

I think teachers often mistakenly think of learning over time as a linear function, but I think it’s probably more exponential, as the more you know the easier it is to learn more, often called the Matthew effect.

For some students and classes there is a point whereby we have to cut our losses. Unfortunately we have to be pragmatic on the time we spend and there might be some students who do not establish a strong grasp.
